questions.stem: In terms of maximum structural payload, which freighter outlifts the other and by approximately how much: the Boeing 747-8F or the Boeing 777F?
options: Boeing 777F; by approximately 35 tonnes — its longer fuselage compensates for fewer decks
Boeing 747-8F; by approximately 5 tonnes — the two types are nearly matched in payload
Boeing 747-8F; by approximately 35 tonnes — its double-deck wide-body configuration carries significantly more
They are identical — Boeing rated both at approximately 102 tonnes maximum structural payload
questions.why: The 747-8F's max structural payload is ~137.7 t vs the 777F's ~103.4 t — a ~34-tonne advantage from its main deck, upper deck, and larger bulk hold combined.
questions.deepDive: The 747-8F remains the world's largest commercial freighter by maximum structural payload at approximately 137.7 tonnes, versus the 777F's 103.4 tonnes — a ~34-tonne advantage. The 747-8F's main deck, upper deck, and bulk hold combine to roughly 858 cubic metres of volume. However, the 777F wins on point-to-point economics when payload demand doesn't fill the 747's belly: lower crew costs (two pilots), more fuel-efficient engines per tonne-km at 80–90% load factors, and a range of ~9,000 km versus the 747-8F's ~8,130 km. Airlines like Cargolux and Lufthansa Cargo operate both types strategically — 777Fs for high-frequency thinner routes, 747-8Fs for the densest lanes where filling the upper deck justifies the cost.

questions.stem: Anchorage Ted Stevens International (ANC) consistently ranks among the world's top 5 cargo airports by throughput tonnage despite having almost no significant local freight market. What makes it operationally indispensable on transpacific routes?
options: It operates the world's largest FedEx sort hub for overnight domestic US redistribution
Its location on the great-circle transpacific path allows freighters to refuel or swap crews with minimal route deviation
ANC has North America's longest commercial runway, enabling max-weight 747-8F operations year-round
Bilateral air services agreements allow foreign-flag freighters to carry US domestic cargo through ANC
questions.why: ANC sits almost exactly on the shortest great-circle path between North Asian hubs (ICN, NRT, PVG) and US East Coast gateways, enabling tech stops that add minimal distance while allowing refuelling and crew swaps.
questions.deepDive: Anchorage sits at roughly 61°N, and the great-circle route from major North Asian cargo hubs to US East Coast gateways passes within a few hundred kilometres of ANC. A tech stop adds minimal deviation — often under 300 km — while allowing freighters to top up fuel (extending effective range beyond normal limits) or swap flight crews to comply with duty-time regulations. The airport operates 24/7 with no curfews, no significant slot constraints, dedicated cargo terminals, and bonded warehouse facilities. FedEx, UPS, Atlas Air, Polar Air and multiple Asian cargo carriers use ANC as a tech stop or mid-route crew change point, making its throughput almost entirely transiting freight rather than local origin-destination cargo.

questions.stem: DSV's acquisition of DB Schenker, completed in 2025 for approximately $14–15 billion, was the largest freight forwarding M&A deal in history. What was the primary commercial rationale from DSV's perspective?
options: To acquire Schenker's European rail network and become the leading Europe–China corridor rail operator
To add Schenker's #1 air freight tonnage ranking to a DSV air forwarding operation seen as weak
To gain scale in European contract logistics and road freight, narrowing the gap on Kuehne+Nagel's top-ranked ocean and air forwarding position
To acquire Schenker's automotive just-in-time supply chain business and matching ERP systems
questions.why: DSV was strong in ocean/air forwarding but lacked scale in European contract logistics and road freight — Schenker's core strengths — and the combined entity now challenges Kuehne+Nagel on total forwarding volume.
questions.deepDive: The DSV-Schenker deal (approximately $14–15B, completed 2025) created the world's #2 freight forwarder by revenue behind Kuehne+Nagel. Schenker's primary value to DSV was its massive European contract logistics (3PL warehousing, value-added services) and road freight network — areas where DSV had limited capability despite being a dominant ocean and air forwarder. Schenker also added significant cross-border European rail forwarding capacity. The combined entity now challenges K+N on ocean forwarding TEU volume and DHL on European logistics scale. This continues the decade-long consolidation trend: fewer but larger forwarders can build proprietary digital visibility platforms, automate procurement, and offer shippers single-contract global coverage — advantages that compound with scale.

questions.stem: In an ocean freight Minimum Quantity Commitment (MQC) contract, a shipper commits to 10,000 FEU annually but ships only 7,000 FEU by year-end. What is the standard commercial consequence under most MQC arrangements?
options: The carrier refunds the shipper proportionally to the 30% shortfall
The shipper pays dead freight on the 3,000 unshipped FEU — typically the base rate minus the carrier's saved variable costs
The contract automatically rolls the shortfall volume into the following year
The shipper forfeits its contracted rate and must rebook remaining volume at prevailing spot rates
questions.why: Dead freight penalises the shortfall: the shipper pays the net revenue loss — contracted base rate minus the variable costs the carrier avoided by not loading the missing boxes (typically 40–70% of base rate).
questions.deepDive: MQC (Minimum Quantity Commitment) contracts became standard in container shipping after post-COVID spot market volatility of 2021–2023 made carriers wary of unprotected capacity commitments. The shipper commits to a minimum TEU/FEU volume per quarter or year; the carrier reserves that capacity and typically grants a lower FAK or NAC rate. Dead freight — the shortfall penalty — is calculated as the contracted freight rate minus the variable cost savings the carrier avoids by not loading (roughly fuel per slot, port dues, handling). This net figure is typically 40–70% of base rate in practice. MQC contracts specify the calculation methodology, measurement period, and whether prior over-shipments earn credit. Post-peak (2023–2024), carriers became significantly more aggressive in enforcing shortfall provisions as spot rates normalised and contractual discipline became more valuable to them.

questions.stem: Hau Lee's seminal 1997 paper identified four structural causes of the bullwhip effect in supply chains. Which of the following is NOT one of them?
options: Demand signal processing — each supply chain tier amplifies forecasts based on upstream order data rather than end-customer demand
Order batching — companies order periodically in large lots rather than continuously, magnifying small demand shifts into large upstream swings
Price fluctuation — forward buying during promotions and de-stocking after them create artificial demand waves
Transportation network congestion increasing transit time variability along the supply chain
questions.why: Lee's four causes are demand signal processing, order batching, price fluctuation, and shortage gaming. Transportation variability worsens replenishment uncertainty but is a compounding factor, not one of the four structural drivers.
questions.deepDive: Hau Lee's 1997 HBR article 'The Bullwhip Effect in Supply Chains' (co-authored with V. Padmanabhan and Seungjin Whang) identified four root causes: (1) demand signal processing — each tier forecasts from upstream orders rather than end-customer POS data, amplifying noise; (2) order batching — periodic large-lot ordering creates lumpy demand even when end demand is smooth; (3) price fluctuation — promotional forward buying and subsequent de-stocking create artificial demand cycles; (4) shortage gaming — buyers over-order during supply crunches expecting allocation cuts. Transportation variability worsens the effect by lengthening lead times and increasing safety stock requirements, but it is not one of Lee's four structural causes. The practical remedies: share POS data upstream, move to continuous replenishment, stabilise pricing, and use allocation mechanisms that discourage gaming.

questions.stem: John Rawls and Jürgen Habermas both developed theories of public reason and political legitimacy, but their approaches diverge fundamentally. What best captures the core difference?
options: Rawls restricts public reason to constitutional essentials; Habermas extends discourse ethics to all collective political decisions
Habermas grounds legitimacy in ideal speech conditions; Rawls grounds it in an overlapping consensus among holders of competing reasonable comprehensive doctrines
Rawls accepts religious arguments in public reason if a secular translation is provided; Habermas categorically excludes them
Habermas rejects the original position entirely, arguing historical social practice — not hypothetical choice — generates normative standards
questions.why: Habermas locates legitimacy in procedural discourse conditions (the ideal speech situation); Rawls locates it substantively in overlapping consensus — political agreement that doesn't require shared comprehensive doctrines.
questions.deepDive: The Rawls-Habermas exchange (they traded papers in the Journal of Philosophy in 1995) is one of the sharpest debates in modern political philosophy. Both accept that liberal democracies need a shared basis for political argument beyond any one religion or metaphysics. Rawls' 'public reason' limits citizens to justifications that all reasonable people could accept, producing an 'overlapping consensus' across different comprehensive doctrines on basic political terms. Habermas' 'discourse ethics' instead specifies procedural conditions: legitimate decisions emerge from communication where all affected parties can participate equally in undistorted dialogue. Rawls is substantive — he pre-loads the content of public reason; Habermas is procedural — he specifies only the conditions of valid discourse. Habermas criticised Rawls for making the original position too thick with liberal assumptions that beg the very questions being decided.

questions.stem: The Coase Theorem holds that private bargaining produces efficient resource allocation regardless of initial property rights assignment. What are the necessary conditions most commonly identified for this result to hold?
options: Zero transaction costs, clearly defined and enforceable property rights, and no significant wealth effects between parties
Perfect competition in all relevant markets and symmetric information among all bargaining parties
Property rights assigned to the highest-valuing party and government arbitration available as a backstop mechanism
Absence of externalities and the presence of at least three competing bidders for each contested resource
questions.why: Coase's insight requires zero (or negligible) transaction costs and well-defined property rights — the theorem's real power is its contrapositive: when those conditions fail, initial rights assignment matters for efficiency.
questions.deepDive: Ronald Coase introduced the insight in 'The Problem of Social Cost' (1960) that with zero transaction costs and clear property rights, parties bargain to an efficient outcome regardless of who initially holds the right. The theorem's deeper lesson is its own limits: because transaction costs (identifying parties, negotiating, monitoring compliance, enforcing agreements) are almost always significant in practice, the initial assignment of rights does matter for efficiency. This explains why externalities cause market failures and why institutions — liability rules, regulation, Pigouvian taxes — can improve on unassisted markets. Coase himself reportedly resented the 'Coase Theorem' label because his point was that zero transaction costs are imaginary and the practical insight is about designing real institutions for high-transaction-cost reality. The wealth-effect caveat: different rights assignments change who can afford to pay for the optimal outcome, so the identity of the efficient allocation can itself depend on the initial distribution.

questions.stem: Beyoncé's 2016 visual album 'Lemonade' sparked an industry-wide debate on streaming exclusivity. What was the distinctive release strategy that set it apart from conventional album launches?
options: It was released as a Spotify exclusive for 72 hours before going to all platforms simultaneously
It debuted as a one-hour HBO film before any music was available digitally, then remained a Tidal exclusive for several weeks
It was released simultaneously on CD, vinyl, and download but permanently withheld from all streaming platforms
Beyoncé sold it exclusively through her own website on a pay-what-you-want model, bypassing all major distributors
questions.why: Lemonade premiered on HBO on April 23, 2016, as a film before any audio release, then moved to Tidal exclusively — forcing the industry to articulate what platform exclusivity windows were actually worth.
questions.deepDive: Beyoncé's 'Lemonade' (April 23, 2016) set a precedent by debuting as a one-hour HBO special — blending music videos, poetry, and narrative film — before the audio was available on any streaming platform except Tidal, co-owned by Jay-Z. The exclusivity window created a major industry debate: labels and artists began modelling how platform-exclusive windows could drive subscription sign-ups before broader releases. The format influenced subsequent high-profile exclusives: Frank Ocean's 'Blonde' (Apple Music exclusive, August 2016), Kanye West's 'The Life of Pablo' (initially Tidal exclusive), and broader windowing discussions that continue today. The release also demonstrated that an album could be a multi-platform audio-visual event rather than simply a collection of songs — reshaping how major artists conceived of release campaigns and what platforms were willing to pay for exclusivity rights.

questions.stem: The Congress of Vienna (1814–15) is considered the prototype of the modern 'concert of great powers.' Which organizing principle most distinguished it from prior peace conferences and shaped European order for the following 40 years?
options: Collective security — signatories committed to military intervention against any state that attacked a congress member
Legitimism — the restoration of pre-Napoleonic dynastic rulers as the primary basis for redrawing European frontiers
The principle of unanimous consent — any territorial change required the agreement of all five great powers
Self-determination of peoples — frontiers were redrawn to align with linguistic and ethnic majorities where feasible
questions.why: Metternich's 'legitimism' — restoring ancien régime dynasties as the organising principle for borders — was Vienna's foundational doctrine, rolling back revolutionary and Napoleonic changes in favour of hereditary order.
questions.deepDive: The Congress of Vienna (September 1814–June 1815) convened Austria (Metternich), Prussia (Hardenberg), Russia (Tsar Alexander I), Britain (Castlereagh/Wellington), and restored France (Talleyrand). Metternich's guiding principle of 'legitimism' held that pre-Napoleonic dynasties had a natural right to their thrones: Bourbons to France and Spain, Habsburgs to northern Italy, the House of Orange to the Netherlands. The resulting Concert of Europe proved remarkably durable — no general European war until the Crimea (1853) and no systemic breakdown until 1914. Self-determination (the principle that reshaped borders after 1918) was exactly what Vienna rejected as a Jacobin-revolutionary idea. The Congress also established a consultative norm among great powers — periodic congresses to manage disputes — representing the first institutionalised multilateral diplomacy system in European history.

questions.stem: The 2018 Aktau Convention resolved the longstanding dispute over whether the Caspian Sea is a 'sea' or a 'lake' under international law. What unusual hybrid legal classification did it introduce?
options: It was formally classified as an international sea under UNCLOS, granting each of the five littoral states a 200-nautical-mile exclusive economic zone
It was designated a sui generis body: seabed resources divided by equidistant median lines (as a sea) but surface waters treated as a shared lake open to all five states
It was declared a condominium — all five states share equal ownership of both seabed and surface resources with no exclusive national zones
Its northern portion was classified as a sea under Russian and Kazakhstani jurisdiction; its southern portion as a lake under Iranian sovereign control
questions.why: The Aktau Convention split the difference: seabed (oil, gas) divided by median lines; surface waters remain shared — critically barring non-littoral naval powers such as NATO from entering.
questions.deepDive: The Caspian's legal status mattered enormously because UNCLOS applies to 'seas' (granting 200nm EEZs) while international law for enclosed lakes defaults to bilateral/multilateral agreements. The five littoral states — Russia, Azerbaijan, Kazakhstan, Turkmenistan, Iran — agreed at Aktau in August 2018: seabed resources (offshore oil and gas fields including Shah Deniz, Kashagan, and Turkmen deposits) are divided by equidistant median lines, while surface waters are treated as a shared lake open to all five states' shipping and fishing. Crucially, the treaty explicitly bars military vessels of non-littoral states — preventing NATO navies from entering — preserving both Russian and Iranian strategic interests in the basin. The classification is called 'sui generis' (of its own kind) precisely because it does not map onto existing UNCLOS or lake-law categories, representing a pragmatic diplomatic invention tailored to the competing interests involved.
